newsitem.title: USA: Levitt opposes "diluted" pay-to-play bans on lawyers.
newsitem.headline: Levitt opposes "diluted" pay-to-play bans on lawyers.

text.p: Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt said Thursday he would not accept a "diluted" alternative to proposed new ethical standards for municipal bond attorneys.

The SEC head also told reporters, after announcing formation of a panel of leading lawyers to lobby the American Bar Association to ban the practice of making political contributions in exchange for legal work on bond issues, that he would be willing to address the body on the issue.
"We would not want a proposal that is so diluted that it lacks any substance," Levitt said when asked about an alternative proposal being developed by an ABA discipline committee.
Levitt backs a recent resolution by the prestigious Association of the Bar of the City of New York on the issue.
The City bar recommended that if a lawyer contributes to an elected municipal official, the attorney and his or her firm may not do public finance business with that locality for two years.

Speaking before a bond-industry seminar Thursday, Levitt announced the formation of a panel of leading lawyers, headed by former Central Intelligence Agency and Federal Bureau of Investigation head William Webster. The panel will lobby the ABA to end the practice at its August meeting.

Paul Maco, director of the SEC's office of municipal securities, said the panel will unveil next week a statement signed by its members and other leading securities lawyers that expresses the reform aims.

The statement says pay-to-play practices undermine the integrity of the securities markets, and notes bond dealers voluntarily condemned the practice in 1993 before a formal ban applying to the dealers was enacted.

The statement goes on to urge national, state and local bar associations "to endorse in principle the condemnation of political contributions by lawyers or law firms that influence or appear to influence the award of legal service contracts with respect to municipal securities offerings."
Levitt said the panel will continue its work beyond the August meeting of the American Bar Association, which is expected to debate the New York City bar's proposed "pay-to-play" ban.
"I intend to use them as an advisory group to consult with me in terms of issues affecting America's bond markets," he said.
Levitt noted that he would not ask the U.S. Congress for a legislative solution to the problem.

Asked about an invitation Wednesday to address the ABA's top policy-making body as it considers the play-to-play issue, Levitt said, "I will accept. Even running the risk of being rejected, I think it's important they hear this message."

One bond attorney at the seminar, David Prior of the firm Ballard Spahr Andrews and Ingersoll, said of Levitt's speech, "I think we all agree with his goal of improving the integrity of the municipal market."
However, he said, "I would question his basic premise that there is a serious problem with the pay-to-play." --U.S. Municipal Desk, 212-859-1650
